fields.meaning: Means “not limited to that scope, but extending to a wider scope”.
examples: Applications are accepted not only on weekdays but also on Saturdays and Sundays.
These days, ice cream seems to sell well not only in summer but in winter too.
* It is not only children who get absorbed in video games.
* I am surely not the only one who thinks the president's way of doing things is strange.
Not only in Japan
This novel is famous not only in Japan but also abroad.
fields.explain: ◎ Expresses that something applies not only within that scope but within an even wider scope.
fields.notes:
examples: 1. この食堂は、学生に限らず、誰でも利用できる。
This cafeteria can be used by anyone, not only students.
2. 今回に限らず、田中さんにはいつもお世話になっている。
Not only this time—Mr. Tanaka always helps me out.

fields.meaning:
「～が一番いい・～がいちばんいい方法だ。」客観的な事実ではなくて、話者が主観的に言うときに使う。
~ is the best / is the best way.
This structure is used when the speaker wants to express their subjective impression rather than an objective fact. | Nothing beats…, the best thing is…
examples: Designer wanted. Experienced applicants only.
Free only for those aged 65 and over.
Only reports written on a computer are accepted.
Eating and drinking in the classroom is permitted only during summer vacation.
It is not only young people whose ability to write kanji is declining.
Movies really are best watched in a movie theater.
fields.notes: Used to assert that 「…が一番だ」 (“…is the best”). Often preceded by 「…なら／たら」.

examples: Identification must be presented when using the service.
When concluding the contract, please check its contents thoroughly.
When I entered school, I was supported by many people.
On taking up my new post, I would like to extend my greetings to you all.
Consent is required upon registration.
When I was admitted to the hospital, several precautions were explained to me.
fields.explain:
Used in official documents, speeches, user guides, and contracts.
Following a Sino-Japanese noun, it creates a ceremonial nuance: ご利用に際して／開館に際して.
Accompanies requests, rules, and ceremonial expressions of thanks/apology.

• Establishes the point in time when an important event begins/takes place, to attach notes, thanks, or requests.
• More formal in nuance than ～とき, close to ～にあたって but leaning toward “the time it takes place”/ceremony.
• Often used with: 入学／卒業／ご利用／ご登録／契約／開業／赴任／受賞 など.
• Rarely used for unexpected negative incidents; if negative, consider the more neutral ～際に (さいに).
fields.notes:
• In speeches: “この場をお借りして” often goes with “就任に際し”.
• The polite variant “～に際しまして” is common in service/IT notices when displaying terms and conditions.
• For unexpected negative events (事故・災害), prefer “際に/とき”; “に際して” sounds dry and unnatural.
meaning_vi: On the occasion of…, at the time of/when… (formal)
examples: 1. ①　受験に際しては、必ず受験票を持参してください。
2. ②　〈大学の掲示板〉奨学金の申し込みに際して、以下のような条件があります。よく確かめた上で、申し込みをしてください。
meaning_vi: ～（特別(とくべつ)なこと）の前(まえ)に、～のときに
When
examples: 1. 就職に際して、多くの先輩にお世話になった。
When I got a job, I received a lot of help from many seniors.
2. 黒田氏はアメリカ大塗料来日際し、通訳を務めた。
Mr. Kuroda served as interpreter when the U.S. president came to Japan.
3. 海外駐在員を選ぶに際しては、仕事の能力だけではなく性格も考慮すべきだ。
When selecting staff to be posted overseas, one should consider not only their work ability but also their personality.
4. 「ここに入院に際しての注意事項が書いてありますから、読んでおいてください」
“The precautions for hospital admission are written here, so please read them beforehand.”
meaning_vi: When starting…, while…
explain: Means at the point of starting some special matter, or while that matter is in progress.
It is a solemn style. Formal, stiff language.
examples: 1. お申し込みに際しては、写真が必要となります。
A photo is required when applying.
2. A氏は日本を訪問するに際し、喜びを語った。
Mr. A spoke of his joy on the occasion of visiting Japan.
mistakes: Using it for small everyday actions (毎朝起きるに際して…) → unnatural; use とき.
Confusing it with にあたって: exam questions often require choosing the appropriate nuance (preparation vs. ceremony).
Forgetting the polite variant in formal documents: you should use に際し／に際しまして.

rows: Emphasizes the point in time of a ceremony/important event
<ruby>入社<rt>にゅうしゃ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>際<rt>さい</rt></ruby>して<ruby>挨拶<rt>あいさつ</rt></ruby>する。
<ruby>開業<rt>かいぎょう</rt></ruby>にあたって<ruby>計画<rt>けいかく</rt></ruby>を<ruby>練<rt>ね</rt></ruby>る。
<ruby>来日<rt>らいにち</rt></ruby>の<ruby>際<rt>さい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>ください。

fields.meaning: To do to the end, persevere…
examples: Whatever you have decided, see it through to the end.
He ran the full 42.195 km in his first marathon.
After thinking it through thoroughly, I decided to quit the company and go independent.
Mr. A survived the war years, and after the war he devoted himself to rebuilding his homeland.
worry to the utmost / endure to the end / persevere to the end / be utterly at a loss
Having endured a difficult period to the end, I finally achieved success.
fields.explain:
Used when you want to honor effort and will: has a positive, encouraging nuance.
Not used for instantaneous actions/actions lacking duration (×笑いぬく). Suitable for continuous/long-term actions.
Often appears in slogans, self-introductions, and inspirational writing: やりぬく力,最後までやりぬく.
The kanji抜く is often used in formal writing; kana ぬく is friendlier and softer.

• Expresses doing something “to the end, completely” through perseverance and overcoming difficulties: Vます + ぬく = do V to the end.
• Nuance: emphasizes a long process with many challenges; the speaker evaluates the effort highly.
• Unlike simple “完了/completion”, 〜ぬく implies persistent will and endurance (耐える、努力する、守る...).
• Often used with verbs expressing prolonged effort: 耐える・守る・戦う・走る・生きる・考える・やる・読み/書き（large amounts/difficult）.
fields.notes:
• “考えぬいた末（すえ）に” is a common written-language phrase, expressing a process of careful thought before making a decision.
• “〜ぬく” can be used in the potential form if the base verb has a potential form: 耐えぬける is unnatural; use 耐えきれる? => For “able to endure”, 耐えきれる/耐え切れる is more natural.
• In PR/recruitment: “困難に立ち向かい、最後までやりぬく人材を求めます。”
explain: ◎ Not giving up, continuing to the end.
examples: 1. これが、彼らが考え抜いて出した結論だった。
This was the conclusion they reached after thinking it through thoroughly.
2. 途中で何度かあきらめかけたが、最後まで走り抜いた。
I almost gave up several times, but in the end I ran all the way.
──────
1. ①　初めてのマラソンは思ったん以上にきつかったけど、最後まで走り抜くことができて、大満足です。
2. ②　〈コーヒー店で〉選び抜かれた豆だけを使った最高級の味を香りをお楽しみください。 meaning_vi: To do everything completely and fully, through a whole process or action.
Emphasizes the sense of completion after enduring hardship. ⏐ examples: 1. 大変な仕事でも、やり抜く自信があります。
Even if the work is hard, I am confident I can see it through to the end.
2. 彼はあきらめずにゴールまで走り抜いた。
He didn't give up and ran all the way to the finish line.
mistakes: Confusing it with “〜ぬ” (archaic negative: 行かぬ). “〜ぬく” is a completion/perseverance suffix, not a negative.
Using it with punctual verbs → unnatural: ×驚きぬく, ×気づきぬく.
Confusing the nuance with 〜きる: 〜きる = completion; 〜ぬく = completion after overcoming difficulties. The JLPT often asks you to distinguish them.
Forgetting to write the kanji: “抜く” is common in formal written language; however, kana “ぬく” is still correct.

rows: Do to the end, overcome difficulties
Focuses on the completed result, not necessarily involving difficulty
Emphasizes holding firm to a stance/action
<ruby>主義<rt>しゅぎ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>貫<rt>つらぬ</rt></ruby>き<ruby>通<rt>とお</rt></ruby>す
Leans toward pouring in all one's strength and heart
<ruby>患者<rt>かんじゃ</rt></ruby>のために<ruby>尽<rt>つ</rt></ruby>くす
Different meaning (intransitive verb), not a completion pattern

examples: The report must be submitted by tomorrow.
We must keep our promises.
We must make this project succeed, no matter what.
Support for the disaster-stricken areas must be provided urgently.
Rules must be observed.
fields.explain:
Used in formal statements, pledges, regulatory documents, and political statements/speeches.
In natural conversation, consider using ～なきゃ/～なくちゃ/～ないと instead.
The subject is usually “I/we/an organization”; directed at the listener, it can easily feel like a command.

• Expresses strong obligation: rules, responsibilities, self-imposed duties.
• Formal/classical nuance, sounds stiffer than ～なければならない; somewhat literary/rhetorical in tone.
• In everyday spoken language it is usually replaced by ～なきゃ／～なくちゃ／～なければならない.
fields.notes:
• In headlines/slogans: ～せねばならない creates a strong, concise rhythm.
• Masculine/old-fashioned colloquial contracted form: ～ねばならん (not formal).
• With “～ねば”, “ならない” can be omitted in a rallying style: 守らねば！ (strong, archaic nuance).
mistakes: Wrong conjugation with する: “しねばならない” → incorrect; it must be “せねばならない”.
Confusing the nuance with ざるを得ない: the latter means “reluctantly having no choice”, not an obligation based on rules.
Using it in casual conversation → sounds stiff/theatrical; use なきゃ/ないと instead.
The JLPT often tests recognition of 未然形: 書く→書かねばならない; 食べる→食べねばならない.

rows: <ruby>守<rt>まも</rt></ruby>らなければならない。
<ruby>守<rt>まも</rt></ruby>らなくてはならない。
<ruby>延期<rt>えんき</rt></ruby>せざるを<ruby>得<rt>え</rt></ruby>ない。

fields.connection: V/A plain form + のではないか / N・Na + なのではないか
examples: I think there may come a time in the future when robots provide nursing care.
I wonder if she's still undecided about studying abroad.
fields.explain: ◎ An expression of conjecture about something.
fields.notes: Attaches to plain-style expressions and expresses the speaker's conjectural judgment, along the lines of 「はっきりそうだと断定はできないが、おそらく…ではないだろうか」 (“I can't say for certain that it is so, but perhaps…”). The speaker's degree of certainty is lower than with 「だろう」.

fields.connection: V plain form + のも + (は)もっともだ / N + も
examples: Since your promise was broken, it's only natural that you're angry.
If it's your first presentation, it's only natural to be nervous.
He had been staying up all night for days on end, so it's no wonder he made a mistake.
With prices rising this much, it's only natural that there is discontent.
It's just a child, so it's only natural that it cries.
fields.explain:
Usually follows a part stating the reason (～から/～ので/状況説明).
Used for a second or third person; used about yourself it can sound like self-justification, but it is not wrong when reflecting on yourself.
Standard, somewhat objective nuance; suitable for reports/evaluations.

Expresses “(A) is understandable/reasonable/natural”. The speaker judges an action/emotion/state to be reasonable based on the stated circumstances. Sympathetic, justifying nuance.
• Often used for other people's emotions/behavior: 怒る・悲しむ・心配する…
• Unlike command/volition: not used to give orders, only to state a judgment.
• Emphasizes objectivity more than 「～のも無理はない」 (less inclined toward “can't be blamed”).
fields.notes:
• 「もっとも」 is also a conjunction meaning “however/that said”: もっとも、例外もある。 Do not confuse it with 「もっともだ」.
• The tense/modifier form can change: ～のももっともだった／～のももっともだろう to adjust tense/degree of certainty.
• The direct negative 「もっともではない」 is rarely used; it is usually replaced with another, softer pattern.
mistakes: Confusing it with 「もっとも」 (conjunction) → 「だ」 is needed to make it a -だ adjective.
Attaching it directly to na-adjectives/N without 「な/である」: you need Aなのも/Nなのも or であるのも.
Using it to criticize others sounds contradictory: this pattern is essentially about sympathy/reasonableness.
Changing the subject between the reason part and the main clause makes the reference ambiguous (keep it consistent).

rows: Nothing strange about it/can't be blamed
Emphasizes that it is unavoidable, more emotional
<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しすぎて、<ruby>遅<rt>おく</rt></ruby>れるのも<ruby>無理<rt>むり</rt></ruby>はない
<ruby>当然<rt>とうぜん</rt></ruby>だ / <ruby>当<rt>あ</rt></ruby>たり<ruby>前<rt>まえ</rt></ruby>だ
Direct and stronger; can sound judgmental
<ruby>失敗<rt>しっぱい</rt></ruby>して<ruby>落<rt>お</rt></ruby>ち<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>むのは<ruby>当然<rt>とうぜん</rt></ruby>だ
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>怒<rt>おこ</rt></ruby>るのも<ruby>道理<rt>どうり</rt></ruby>だ

examples: It is possible in theory, but difficult to realize.
It is close on the map, but it takes time because it's a mountain road.
On paper, he is a full-time employee.
According to the statistics, the economy is recovering.
Legally, discrimination is prohibited.
fields.explain:
Usually followed by a second clause expressing a contrasting reality or adding context.
Style: neutral → formal; suitable for documents, reports, and news.
Not used to indicate a sequence in time/of actions (that is a different meaning of上で).

～の上では states a judgment “from the standpoint of A / according to A / on paper…”, emphasizing a theoretical perspective, documents, figures, or maps. Common implication: reality may differ (contrast between theory and reality).
• Semantic domain: 理論・記録・統計・法律・書類・地図・規則 など.
• Often used in contrasting pairs: Nの上では～が、実際は～／現場では～.
• Different from 「上で(うえで)＝after/in order to」; here it means “in terms of”.
fields.notes:
• 「見かけの上では」「形式の上では」「制度の上では」 are phrases common in journalistic writing.
• In spoken language, 「上では」 can drop 「は」 and become 「上で」, but this is easily confused with the other meaning; keep 「は」 when writing.
• Precede it with a nominalized phrase to make the aspect clear: 実験結果の上では／理屈の上では…
mistakes: Confusing it with 「Vた上で」: exam questions often set traps to distinguish “in terms of” vs. “after”.
Omitting 「は」 after 「上で」 makes the meaning unclear; on the exam, choose 「上では」 for the meaning “on paper”.
Using it with nouns that cannot be an “aspect” (e.g., 人の上では) → unnatural.

rows: Neutral, does not imply a contrast with reality
<ruby>統計<rt>とうけい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>しては<ruby>詳<rt>くわ</rt></ruby>しい
<ruby>研究<rt>けんきゅう</rt></ruby>において<ruby>重要<rt>じゅうよう</rt></ruby>だ
<ruby>確認<rt>かくにん</rt></ruby>した<ruby>上<rt>うえ</rt></ruby>で<ruby>提出<rt>ていしゅつ</rt></ruby>する
<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>する<ruby>上<rt>うえ</rt></ruby>で<ruby>大切<rt>たいせつ</rt></ruby>だ

examples: Joking aside, let's talk about our future policy.
Setting aside whether it will produce results, we should first put it into action.
Price aside, safety is our top priority.
Setting aside whether or not he is responsible, solving the problem comes first.
Design aside, the functionality is flawless.
Setting aside the question of cost, where would you most like to go right now?
fields.explain:
Usually placed at the beginning of a sentence, as a signal of a transition/priority.
Used when there are two parallel criteria/topics but you want to focus on B.
Avoid applying it bluntly to a sensitive target, as it can come across as rude to the listener.

• “Setting aside/not discussing N for now, (let's) discuss/prioritize B.” Used for a topic shift to something more important/urgent.
• Nuance of actively steering the conversation/discussion; somewhat polite, leaning toward written language, meetings, and presentations.
• Different from ignoring something permanently: it is set aside “temporarily” and can be returned to later.
fields.notes:
• Origin “措く/置く”: to put aside → a natural nuance of changing direction.
• In presentations, it can be followed by “まず/先に/本題に入る”.
• Easily combined with pairs of contrasting criteria: 値段vs品質, 感情vs事実, 理想vs現実.
mistakes: Using it in place of absolute “exclusion” → wrong nuance. ～はさておき means “set aside for now”, not “unrelated”.
Failing to nominalize an interrogative clause: × 行けるかはさておき → ◯ 行けるかどうかはさておき.
Placing it after an overly long phrase loses its switching effect; it should be placed early, at the beginning of the sentence.

rows: Set topic N aside for now
Nuance of steering the conversation; more formal
<ruby>冗談<rt>じょうだん</rt></ruby>はさておき、<ruby>本題<rt>ほんだい</rt></ruby>へ
<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>た<ruby>目<rt>め</rt></ruby>はともかく、<ruby>味<rt>あじ</rt></ruby>はいい
Implies excluding N from the scope of evaluation
<ruby>休日<rt>きゅうじつ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>別<rt>べつ</rt></ruby>として、<ruby>毎日<rt>まいにち</rt></ruby><ruby>早起<rt>はやお</rt></ruby>きだ
Adverb, does not mark a topic

fields.meaning: Speaking of / when it comes to ~
examples: As for this year's goal, it's to win the national tournament, no matter what.
As for her, she doesn't seem to have decided yet whether she'll participate.
I heard there was an earthquake last night. As for me, I was sound asleep and didn't notice it at all.
As for Japan at that time, Buddhism was spreading among the people.
fields.explain: ◎ An expression that presents a topic, used especially when you want to raise an issue to draw everyone's attention to it.

examples: His report received a low evaluation: besides its content, it had many spelling mistakes.
This anime can be fully enjoyed not only by children but by adults as well.
I can speak not only Japanese but also English and Chinese.
We pay close attention not only to safety but also to quality control.
He is not only polite but also always punctual.
Not only students but even local residents are taking part.
fields.explain:
Used when you want to emphasize “A goes without saying, and B also…” to broaden the scope or raise the standard.
Serious, polite style; suitable for reports, articles, and official speeches.
The second clause should have も/まで/さえ to show the extension; avoid creating an “empty” sentence that only states that A is obvious without main information afterward.
Not used to emphasize everyday personal feelings; in casual conversation, ～はもちろん/～は言うまでもなく is more natural.

• Meaning 1: “Let alone…, needless to say…, of course…”, used to present A as obvious and then extend the scope to B, C (… as well).
• Meaning 2: “Not only A but even B/C …” with a nuance emphasizing the degree of inclusiveness, often accompanied by も/まで/さえ in the second clause.
• Feel: formal, leaning toward written language, announcements, and presentations; stronger than ～はもちろん in its “of course” sense.
• Syntax: Part A (before はもとより) is usually a noun. If it is a clause, it must be nominalized with の/こと.
• Logic: A is the basis/obvious → B is also satisfied/included → a general conclusion is stated.
fields.notes:
• Often combined with inclusive words: も・まで・さえ to increase the emphasis.
• “もとより” also has the lexical meaning “from the start/originally”, which differs from this grammar structure; distinguish them by the presence or absence of は.
• In administrative writing/advertising: “安全はもとより、環境にも配慮しています。” is a stock sentence type.
• The A–B order should follow the degree: A is more obvious than B. Reversing them makes it less natural. meaning_vi: Not only, let alone. ⏐ explain: Presents things considered obvious to express the meaning “not only that, but there are also more important or lesser matters”
Used in a serious style typical of written language. ⏐ examples: 1. うちには、車はもとより自転車もないんです。
At my house, there's not only no car but not even a bicycle.
2. レタスはサラダで食べるのはもとより、炒めてもおいしい。
Lettuce is not only good eaten in salads, but also tasty stir-fried.
mistakes: Using it with a verb but forgetting to nominalize: × 努力するはもとより → ○ 努力するのはもとより
Missing an extending particle in the second clause: × Aはもとより、B。 → use Bも/まで/さえ to make the extension clear.
Confusing it with ～はもちろん in terms of style: the JLPT often asks about the more formal nuance of ～はもとより.
Wrong order of degree: the “obvious” information must be placed before はもとより.

rows: Of course A, and B also …
<ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>はもとより、<ruby>海外<rt>かいがい</rt></ruby>でも<ruby>人気<rt>にんき</rt></ruby>だ。
<ruby>英語<rt>えいご</rt></ruby>はもちろん、<ruby>仏語<rt>ふつご</rt></ruby>もできる。
Similar in meaning, often placed at the beginning of a sentence like an adverbial
<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>うまでもなく<ruby>健康<rt>けんこう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>一番<rt>いちばん</rt></ruby>だ。
Far from A, actually B (contrary to expectation)
<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>めるどころか、<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しい。
